text.p: The United States on Tuesday welcomed Croatia's decision to press charges against 12 people for harassing and evicting elderly minority Serbs who returned to their pre-war homes.
"This is a step in the right direction," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
"It's the kind of action that Secretary (of State Madeleine) Albright asked President (Franjo) Tudjman to take, to make sure that people can return to their homes in the Krajina region," he said.
During a weekend visit to Croatia, including the Krajina, Albright criticised Tudjman for treatment of minority Serbs who fled en masse from the Croatian army's 1995 recapture of their rebel area.

In a rare public rebuke, she said the Croatian government "should be ashamed" of how minority Serbs have been treated. She demanded perpetrators be prosecuted and that victims be compensated for the loss of their destroyed and burned homes.

Without such action, Albright said Washington would oppose Zagreb's access to international financial assistance, to U.S. bilateral aid and to membership in international groups, like NATO's "partnership for peace" programme.
Albright urged Tudjman to exercise moral leadership to create conditions for the return and co-existence of Serbs and Croats and said it would be "useful if some arrests were made" in the area.
Tudjman seemed to comply on Monday by giving a conciliatory speech to Serbs in their last, soon-to-be-dissolved enclave of Eastern Slavonia and vowing to protect multi-ethnic life.
Authorities previously blamed the evictions on embittered Croat refugees from Bosnia's 1992-95 war who were resettled in Serb houses near Kostajnica, central Croatia.

The United States has raised the possibility it might back a delay in the return of Eastern Slavonia, which is now under U.N. administration, to Croatian control if Zagreb does not do more to facilitate the safe return of refugees.
Croatia recaptured all other Serb-held territory in a lightning offensive in 1995 and Eastern Slavonia is now home to thousands of Serbs who fled their advance.

The government plans to resettle tens of thousands of displaced people, but for Croats to return to Eastern Slavonia which they fled at the onset of war in 1991, the Serbs who live there must return to their own pre-war homes.
